text: Does the pain worsen when you lift your thumb away from your hand and extend it outward, or when you twist your wrist like turning a doorknob? I also need to know if you have noticed any swelling or a lump on the thumb side of your wrist.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the pain location and aggravating factors, this sounds like De Quervain's tenosynovitis. Do you have a history of repetitive wrist movements or recent trauma to that area?

speaker: Patient
text: I don't do repetitive motions at work, but I did fall on my right outstretched hand about six months ago. That was the only significant trauma I've had to that area.

speaker: Doctor
text: Did the pain start immediately after that fall six months ago, or did it develop gradually over time? Also, does pressing on the bony bump at the base of your thumb reproduce the sharp pain?

speaker: Patient
text: The pain didn't start right after the fall; it actually began about three months ago and has been getting worse since then. Yes, pressing on that bony bump at the base of my thumb definitely reproduces the sharp pain.

speaker: Doctor
text: The delayed onset after trauma and positive tenderness at the radial styloid strongly suggest De Quervain's tenosynovitis. To confirm this, I will perform Finkelstein's test by asking you to make a fist with your thumb tucked inside and then bend your wrist toward your little finger.

speaker: Patient
text: Oh, that movement sends a sharp, shooting pain right up my forearm. It’s definitely the most painful thing you’ve asked me to do so far.

speaker: Doctor
text: That positive Finkelstein's test confirms the diagnosis. DIAGNOSIS READY: De Quervain's tenosynovitis
